title: 137 Effect of arrival fecal egg count on health, performance, and reinfection rate in stocker steers during a 90-d grazing period
content:
Abstract
Forage based beef cattle systems can lend to increased negative interactions with internal parasites leading to decreased growth and performance. The objectives of the study were to determine the impact of arrival parasite load, specifically fecal egg count (FEC), 1) on health and performance and 2) on reinfection rate over a 90-day period in grazing beef steers. Beef steers (n=113) were received on d -1 from a local sale barn and then transported to the H.H. Leveck Research Station. On d -1, shrunk body weights were obtained. On d-0 steers were randomly assigned to 1 of 12 5-acre pastures. It should be noted that the steers (n=113) were part of a larger research project that investigated the effects of supplementing Bovacillus on health, performance, and physiological responses. On d-0, steers were dewormed using fenbendazole (Safe-Guard), vaccinated for BRD related illnesses, and weights were obtained. Overall ADG was calculated by linear regression. Fecal samples were obtained via rectal palpation, on day 0, 14, 28, 56, and 90, and sent to the Merck Lab located in Lawrence, KS for analysis. The cattle were then classified as low, medium, or high arrival FEC based on a 0.5 standard deviation above and below the mean (n=30 LOW, n=50 MED and n=20 HIGH). FEC plus1, to account for 0 counts, were log transformed for analysis. Treatment effects on BRD and performance measures were tested using Poisson distribution, linear regression, using the MIXED procedure of SAS. Reinfection rate was analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS with a fixed effect of Bovacillus treatment, with the repeated effect of day. The mean FEC for each classification were LOW=128.8 EP3G, MED=185.1 EP3G and HIGH=222.7 EP3G (P< 0.05). Overall morbidity was 72.57% with 2.7% mortality. Overall morbidity (LOW=44%, MED=30%, HIGH= 26%) did not differ (P=0.73) by arrival FEC class. There was no difference in ADG based on arrival FEC class. However, there was an interaction (P< 0.05) between TRT and class, such that cattle that received Bovacillus and had high arrival FEC had lower ADG. There was no difference in BW at any period during the trial (P >0.10). Results indicated Bovacillus didn’t impact FEC at any time point (P=0.14). Reinfection rate analysis indicated that all cattle had a reduction in FEC after deworming. Overall, the FEC decreased slightly from day 0 to day 14 for all classes, increased slightly from day 14 to day 28 for all classes, increased from day 28 to day 56 for low and high while remaining the same for medium, and decreased slightly from day 56 to day 90 for low while the remaining classes experienced no difference (P< 0.01). Steers classified with high parasite load, at arrival, remained highest through the trial.
